n: The whole earth is invited to sing a ‘new song’ — fresh praise for a new act of God. A version of this psalm appears when David brought the ark to Jerusalem.
To ‘bless’ God’s name is to praise and honor it. His saving acts should be announced every day, like ongoing good news.

f.g: Proclaim the good news of his deliverance.

n: God’s glory is meant for every people, not just Israel. This anticipates the missionary call to all nations.
The Lord deserves the highest praise and reverence, above any other being people worship.
A wordplay: the nations’ gods (elohim) are mere idols (elilim, ‘nothings’), but the Lord made the heavens.

f.g: Hebrew elilim — ‘worthless things,’ a pun on elohim (gods).

n: Honor, majesty, strength, and beauty are pictured as attendants standing before God in his sanctuary.
‘Give unto the LORD’ — that is, acknowledge and declare his glory and strength. All the families of the earth are invited.
Worshipers bring offerings as they enter the temple courts. In ancient Israel no one came before the King empty-handed.
Worship God in holy splendor — perhaps in sacred clothing or a holy manner. ‘Fear before him’ means tremble in reverence.
The message to share with every nation: the Lord is King! His rule brings stability and fair judgment.
All creation — heavens, earth, sea, and everything in it — is called to celebrate.
Fields and forests join in. Creation itself rejoices when God comes to set things right.

f.w: all the trees of the wood rejoice

n: The reason: the Lord is coming to judge the world fairly and faithfully. For Latter-day Saints this looks forward to Christ’s Second Coming and millennial reign.

f.w: he cometh to judge the earth
